articles.summary: An eight-year-old boy in Indiana has received recognition from a volunteer fire department after noticing a smoking camper trailer and alerting people
articles.body: An eight-year-old boy in Indiana has received recognition from a volunteer fire department after noticing a smoking camper trailer and alerting people nearby, helping ensure firefighters were called before the situation became more serious. According to local broadcaster Eagle Country 99.3 and the Blooming Grove Volunteer Fire Department, Carter Hicks was presented with a department patch and a Certificate of Recognition for his actions. The incident occurred during the summer, when Carter noticed smoke coming from a camper trailer that appeared to be catching fire. Rather than ignore the warning signs, he informed people in the vicinity, prompting a fire department response. The department later honoured Carter for his awareness and initiative, highlighting how his concern for another person’s property helped bring attention to a potentially dangerous situation.A small act with a potentially big impactFor firefighters, recognising the early signs of an emergency can make a significant difference. Smoke coming from a trailer can indicate a developing fire, and drawing attention to it quickly gives people an opportunity to respond before the situation escalates.In Carter’s case, his decision to alert those nearby helped ensure the problem was noticed and brought to the attention of emergency responders. The department’s recognition focused not only on his quick thinking but also on his concern for the safety and property of others. His actions demonstrated how remaining alert and responding responsibly can make a meaningful difference during potentially dangerous situations. Details about the cause of the smoke, the extent of any damage and whether anyone was injured were not included in the initial local news report.Fire department recognises community spiritMembers of the Blooming Grove Volunteer Fire Department presented Carter with the patch and certificate during a recognition ceremony held on the Saturday before the October 8 report. The department praised the youngster’s sense of responsibility, noting that community members can play an important role in identifying hazards and alerting others, even without formal emergency training.The recognition also carried a broader message about public service: making a difference does not always require specialised equipment or an official role. Paying attention to one’s surroundings and speaking up when something appears unsafe can be valuable contributions to community safety.Why early warnings matterFire safety guidance consistently stresses the importance of treating smoke and other possible signs of fire seriously. The US Fire Administration advises people to get to safety and contact emergency services when they encounter a fire, rather than putting themselves at risk by attempting to tackle it.Carter’s response offered a simple example of that principle. He noticed something unusual, alerted other people and helped bring the situation to the attention of firefighters.At eight years old, he was not expected to fight the fire himself. His contribution came from recognising that something was wrong and making sure others knew about it. His actions also highlight the importance of teaching children to stay calm, recognise potential hazards and seek help from trusted adults or emergency services when dangerous situations arise. The department’s decision to honour him underscores how awareness, responsibility and consideration for others can matter in an emergency, regardless of age.You use AI every day. articles.title: What’s happening at Jantar Mantar? CJP’s ‘cockroaches’ grounded before anti-SIR showdown
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: As planned, the ‘cockroaches’ could not make their way to Jantar Mantar, with the detention of key Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders before
articles.body: NEW DELHI: As planned, the ‘cockroaches’ could not make their way to Jantar Mantar, with the detention of key Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders before they could reach the protest site throwing the outfit’s ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ plans into disarray. Delhi’s sweeping security crackdown, which has reportedly led to over 1,500 detentions across the capital, further dampened the expected turnout at the demonstration against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained by Delhi Police upon arriving at Indira Gandhi International airport from Mumbai.The outfit’s head of legal affairs, Ratna Singh, was also detained.The developments came hours before the outfit’s planned ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ demonstration demanding the removal of Gyanesh Kumar over the Election Commission’s special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The protest, proposed by the CJP despite Delhi Police denying permission, was expected to draw around 20,000 participants. However, the detention of key organisers and the extensive security deployment have majorly affected preparations for the demonstration.CJP leaders detained inside aircraftIn a video shared on social media, Dipke could be heard alleging that Delhi Police personnel entered the aircraft shortly after it landed to detain him and his fellow leaders.“So, you can see that Delhi Police is entering the plane to arrest us. They are all entering the plane. We just landed. All the Delhi Police officers are standing in the aisle. They are trying to arrest us from inside the plane. The entire Delhi Police is getting on the plane. This is the fear of Narendra Modi,” Dipke said.“Not even Indira Gandhi did this during the Emergency. All we wanted to do is a peaceful protest, and they are picking us up from the flight like we are criminals,” he added.In the same video, CJP leaders Ranka and Das could be heard raising slogans of “Bharat Mata Ki Jai” and “Inquilab Zindabad”.The group termed the detentions "illegal" and alleged that the police action was aimed at preventing its leaders from reaching Jantar Mantar for the planned demonstration.YouTuber Dhruv Rathee detained ahead of protestAlmost an hour before the CJP leadership arrived at Delhi airport, the outfit’s supporter and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was reportedly detained by Gurugram Police from his residence in Sector 56.Rathee, who lives abroad, had travelled to participate in the demonstration, according to the information shared by the outfit. His reported detention added to the uncertainty surrounding the protest, which had already triggered heightened security arrangements across Delhi and its adjoining areas.READ ALSO: 'Nalayak neta': BJP accuses Rahul of dragging President into 'street fights', creating 'anarchy'35,000 personnel deployed; internet curbs & traffic restrictionsDelhi was placed under an extensive security blanket ahead of the proposed mobilisation. Around 35,000 police personnel were deployed, with Central Police personnel also present in large numbers around Jantar Mantar and other key locations.The security arrangements included CCTV surveillance and body cameras fitted to the uniforms of deployed personnel.A section of Delhi Police was also designated as the “Pink Force”.Mobile internet services were scheduled to be suspended within a 4-km radius of Jantar Mantar. Authorities also imposed traffic restrictions on roads along Delhi’s borders with Uttar Pradesh and Haryana, as well as routes leading to Jantar Mantar and other parts of New Delhi.Police were coordinating with cab aggregators to regulate vehicle movement, while several trains were reportedly cancelled. The measures formed part of the broader security plan to manage the expected crowds and prevent disruptions across the capital.The scale of the deployment, however, came amid allegations by the CJP that detaining its organisers before they could reach the venue was an attempt to prevent a peaceful protest.Liquor shops shut, commercial activity affectedThe restrictions extended beyond security and transport. Liquor outlets across Delhi were ordered to remain closed on October 9 and 10.Commercial activity was also expected to be affected in parts of the city, particularly around Connaught Place. Market associations in Connaught Place, Sadar Bazar and parts of Karol Bagh and Chandni Chowk confirmed closures for October 10.Markets in Green Park, Sarojini Nagar and Greater Kailash, however, were expected to remain open.The curbs and closures added to the disruption surrounding the proposed demonstration, with authorities preparing for a large turnout even as the detention of key organisers cast doubt on the protest’s eventual scale.Rahul backs demand for CEC’s removal, but Congress skips protestCongress leader Rahul Gandhi reiterated his demand for Gyanesh Kumar’s removal, echoing the central demand of the CJP and other opposition voices opposing the SIR exercise.In a post on X, the former Congress chief wrote: "Gyanesh Kumar will go. This government will go. ""Then the repair of democracy will begin," he added, ending his post with the national flag emoji.However, the Congress stayed away from the CJP’s planned demonstration. Rahul travelled to Chennai to attend an event involving his ally and Tamil Nadu chief minister Vijay.Former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal, meanwhile, had promised to attend the protest with his family. But the detention of key CJP leaders and the heavy security deployment threatened to reduce the gathering well below the turnout initially anticipated by organisers.Kejriwal criticised the Narendra Modi-led Centre over the restrictions, saying: “This is worse than the Emergency, we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi.”CJP appeals for peace amid police restrictionsOn the day of its planned ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ protest, the CJP issued an appeal urging participants to maintain peace, avoid violence and vandalism, follow lawful instructions and ensure that emergency services were not obstructed.The outfit also called on participants to remain peaceful, alert and united. It described the demonstration as an effort to seek accountability over the Election Commission’s special intensive revision of electoral rolls.Despite Delhi Police denying permission for the protest, the CJP had called for a large mobilisation at Jantar Mantar.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A 16-foot Burmese python weighing 147.9 pounds was released after radio-tagging in Florida; US scientists are now testing drones to track invasive snakes across the Everglades
articles.summary: Deep in the Florida Everglades, a vast and difficult landscape, scientists are trying a new way to find invasive Burmese pythons; they are looking from
articles.body: Deep in the Florida Everglades, a vast and difficult landscape, scientists are trying a new way to find invasive Burmese pythons; they are looking from above. Researchers are testing small drones fitted with radio tracking equipment or cameras to locate snakes more efficiently, follow their movements across difficult terrain, and cut the cost of searching from the ground. One female python released after tagging measured 16 feet and weighed 147.9 pounds. In this article, you will learn how the technology works, why pythons are so hard to track, what the scientists hope to gain, and what important questions remain unanswered.How United States scientists use drones to monitor invasive Burmese pythons across the EvergladesThe United States Geological Survey, a federal science agency, is testing a different approach to a long-running wildlife problem. Scientists at its Fort Collins Science Centre are using uncrewed aircraft systems, commonly called drones, to track invasive Burmese pythons and to learn more about how the snakes move across a vast and difficult landscape. The work is described in the center's September 2026 series, which highlights how its projects support sound decision-making. The python project stands out because the agency's own account calls it a novel use of technology that is more commonly applied to monitoring rivers and forests.The 16-foot, 147.9-pound female Burmese python that was radio-taggedA photograph published by the USGS captures the technology at work. In the image, agency biologists operate a small uncrewed aircraft system while University of Florida interns release a newly radio-tagged female Burmese python, 16 feet long and weighing 147.9 pounds, back into the Greater Everglades Ecosystem. The scene shows how the pieces fit together: a snake carrying a radio tag, people on the ground handling it safely, and an aircraft overhead testing how well the tag can be followed from the sky.How radio tracking equipment and cameras improve python detection efficiencyThe agency explains that the aircraft can carry either radio tracking equipment or a camera. The platform is being evaluated as a way to improve detection and tracking efficiency, collect better data, and reduce the labour and operating costs of traditional ground-based monitoring for pythons. In plain terms, a drone can cover wet, thick, hard-to-walk areas far faster than a person on foot, and it can pick up a tagged snake's signal or spot the animal from overhead. If it works well, fewer people would need to spend long hours searching difficult ground.Why Burmese pythons threaten Everglades mammals and why tracking them across difficult terrain is hardThe reason for all this effort is the size of the problem. The United States Geological Survey leads federal research to control the Burmese python, which has become firmly established across the Greater Everglades Ecosystem and poses a serious threat to native wildlife. The snake can grow to more than 17 feet long and is believed to be a key factor in the sharp decline of mammal populations in the region. Finding such a well-camouflaged animal in a huge, wet landscape is slow and costly, which explains why scientists are eager to test aerial tools.How drone training for Department of the Interior scientists brought python tracking to the EvergladesThe idea grew out of a training program. Chris Holmquist-Johnson, a certified instructor in uncrewed aircraft systems for the Department of the Interior, trained a group of Fort Collins Science Centre scientists working in the Florida Everglades about a year before the article was published. Those researchers are now using the technology to track Burmese pythons and are gaining new insight into their movement behaviour. Holmquist-Johnson's main work involves rivers and forests in the western United States, including mapping changes in river channels and surveying thinned forest areas, so the Everglades project shows how skills built in one setting can be carried into another.Why further testing matters for python controlIt is important to read the project for what it is. The agency describes the aircraft as a tool still under evaluation, and the sources do not report measured results, such as how many more snakes are found or how much money is saved. The 16-foot, 147.9-pound snake is a single example from a photograph, not an average, and the agency notes that pythons can grow even longer. As testing continues, the key questions will be how reliably the aircraft locate tagged and untagged snakes, and whether the savings in time and cost hold up across the seasons and the many kinds of habitat in the Everglades.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Our Gen Z deserves better than Emer-GenZ': Shashi Tharoor slams 'war-like deployment' of cops for CJP protest
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Saturday criticised the heavy security deployment across Delhi in the wake of Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP)
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Saturday criticised the heavy security deployment across Delhi in the wake of Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) protest against the Election Commission, describing the arrangements as “war-like” and questioning the restrictions imposed on citizens seeking to demonstrate peacefully.In a post, Tharoor said he had returned to the national capital after 2am and had “rarely seen anything like” the situation unfolding in Delhi, citing checkpoints, concrete barriers, spike strips, the deployment of 22,000 police and paramilitary personnel, cancellation of 250 trains and closure of 45 metro stations. He also referred to reports of young people being detained from their homes and streets in and around Delhi.Tharoor criticised the suspension of internet services in central Delhi, calling it the “most regressive (as well as repressive)” measure. He said freedom of movement had been “completely shackled” and pointed out that Jantar Mantar had been designated as a place where citizens could voice dissent in the heart of the capital.“One is entitled to ask where this extraordinary manpower and urgency disappear when women in our capital need protection,” he said.Questioning what would happen if protesters returned on Monday, Tharoor said those detained would have to be released. “Our GenZ deserves better than an undeclared Emer-GenZ,” he added.Tharoor argued that a government confident in the fairness of elections should welcome questions about the electoral process rather than respond with heavy security measures. “The government should provide answers, not lathis; expression, not repression,” he said.He also said barricades would not restore public faith in the Election Commission and urged the poll body to answer questions raised by citizens. Calling the situation “utterly shameful and unconscionable”, Tharoor said a democracy’s strength was measured by how it treated those who questioned its functioning.Several demonstrators were detained by Delhi Police after gathering at Jantar Mantar amid extensive barricading and heightened security.The CJP had called for a protest over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and demanded Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Police had denied permission for the demonstration, citing security considerations and procedural requirements.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Viola Davis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island; now she and husband Julius Tennon are donating $1.2 million to help local families
articles.summary: For Viola Davis, the place where she grew up remains part of her story, even after a career that has taken her from Rhode Island to Hollywood.
articles.body: For Viola Davis, the place where she grew up remains part of her story, even after a career that has taken her from Rhode Island to Hollywood. The award-winning actress and her husband, Julius Tennon, have announced a $1.2 million investment in Central Falls, the Rhode Island community where Davis once lived. The money will fund a new family engagement centre named after her mother, Mary Alice Davis, whose influence Davis has spoken about in explaining the project. Planned as a permanent base for local services, the centre will bring together food assistance, family support, adult education and employment-related programmes under one roof.A $1.2 million donation honours Viola Davis’s motherThe Mary Alice Davis Family Engagement Center is being developed through the couple’s Davis-Tennon Foundation. Its purpose is to give residents a place to find practical support, whether they need help feeding their families, accessing educational opportunities or preparing for work.For Davis, naming the facility after her mother gives the project a personal connection. She has described the decision as a way of honouring a woman who continued to believe in people through difficult circumstances. The centre, she said, would carry that spirit forward by supporting individuals and creating opportunities for families.As reported by WJAR, the $1.2 million investment was announced on Monday, 20 July 2026. Rather than funding a single short-term initiative, the donation is intended to establish a lasting community resource in Central Falls, a city closely connected to Davis’s childhood.From a childhood in poverty to giving back to her Rhode Island rootsDavis grew up in poverty in Rhode Island, an experience that forms an important part of her personal history. She went on to build a career in film, television and theatre, becoming one of the most widely recognised actors of her generation. Her professional achievements have included major industry awards, but her latest investment focuses on a community far removed from the entertainment business.Central Falls was part of the environment in which Davis spent her early years. The new centre offers a way for her and Tennon to direct resources towards residents who may face financial pressures and limited access to services.The couple's contribution is being made through their foundation, which has an existing connection to Rhode Island. The Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry already serves about 3,000 people each month. The new facility is expected to provide a broader base for that work, alongside services aimed at parents, adults seeking new skills and families looking for guidance.Tennon, who is originally from Austin, Texas, has also expressed his commitment to supporting Rhode Island. Although the state is not his birthplace, he and Davis are directing the investment towards a community that holds particular significance for his wife.What families will be able to access at the new centreThe planned facility will bring several services together in one location. These include a parent resource centre, a parent university and adult empowerment programmes, giving parents and other residents access to information and opportunities for learning.Food assistance will remain part of the work. The expanded Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry is expected to build on a service that already reaches thousands of people monthly. The centre will also provide workforce development and financial literacy programmes, along with family engagement activities, educational workshops and community events.For people looking for help with more than one issue, having these services in the same place could make it easier to find the right support. Someone visiting for food assistance, for example, may also be able to access parenting resources or information about employment training.The facility will also serve as the permanent administrative headquarters of the Davis-Tennon Foundation. This gives the organisation a local base from which to coordinate its activities and maintain its work in the area.Angelo Garcia, chair of the foundation, said, "Whether someone comes seeking food, parenting resources, educational support, workforce training, or guidance through a difficult season, our goal is simple: one place where people are welcomed, connected, and empowered.”How the new centre will support thousands of Rhode Island residentsThe Mary Alice Davis Food Pantry provides an established starting point for the project. Its reported monthly reach of around 3,000 individuals gives an indication of the demand for food assistance in the community and the role the new centre could play in extending that support.The planned expansion will place the pantry within a wider network of family and adult services. Residents will have access not only to food assistance but also to programmes intended to support education, financial understanding and employment prospects.The centre's effectiveness will depend on how these services are delivered and how well they meet local needs once the facility is operating. The announcement sets out the intended range of programmes, although it does not specify an opening date or provide a detailed timetable for their introduction.You use AI every day. articles.summary: The leader of Israel’s Democratic Party, Yair Golan, has described the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei at the start of the US-Israeli
articles.body: The leader of Israel’s Democratic Party, Yair Golan, has described the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei at the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran as a “mistake”, saying it did not serve Israel’s interests.“I think, unequivocally, the elimination of Khamenei, the father, was a mistake,” Golan said on Friday, as cited by Al Jazeera.“Not because he didn’t deserve to die, only because it doesn’t serve the interests of the State of Israel," he added.Golan also described Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s goal of toppling the Iranian government as “unrealistic”.Khamenei, 86, was killed in a US-Israeli airstrike on his leadership compound in Tehran on February 28, the opening day of the war, along with several senior Iranian officials. The Israeli Defence Forces confirmed the strike, which ended his decades-long rule over Iran.He was succeeded by his son, Mojtaba Khamenei, who is believed to be less risk-averse than his father. Since taking over, Mojtaba has largely remained out of public view, communicating mainly through written statements rather than public appearances.During his rule, the elder Khamenei commanded Iran’s armed forces, oversaw domestic repression and directed regional proxy networks. In 2003, he issued a fatwa banning nuclear weapons in Iran, arguing that they violated the tenets of Islam.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Activists Yogendra Yadav and Prashant Bhushan, along with CPI(ML) Liberation general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya and student leader Neha
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Activists Yogendra Yadav and Prashant Bhushan, along with CPI(ML) Liberation general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya and student leader Neha Bora, were detained near INA Market on Saturday while heading to the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) planned ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ protest.The detentions came amid a sweeping crackdown in the national capital ahead of the demonstration against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Election Commission’s special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Earlier, Yadav, a psephologist and former AAP leader, and Bhushan, a lawyer and his former comrade from the Anna Andolan, were seen marching from Jor Bagh towards Dilli Haat-INA alongside AISA's Bora. The group was reportedly on its way to join the CJP protest when police detained them near INA Market.A video showed the psephologist and former AAP leader Yadav walking alongside Bhushan, a lawyer and former AAP colleague, and AISA student leader Neha Bora.The latest detentions came after CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained by Delhi Police shortly after arriving at Indira Gandhi International Airport from Mumbai. articles.title: In 2015, Renée Zellweger paid $3.35 million for a nearly 10-acre Topanga ranch and rebuilt the home down to the studs; she sold it for $6.4 million in 2021, and four years later it returned at $7.995 million
articles.summary: Renée Zellweger’s former Topanga ranch has returned to the market, four years after the actress sold it for $6.4 million.
articles.body: Renée Zellweger’s former Topanga ranch has returned to the market, four years after the actress sold it for $6.4 million. Zellweger bought the nearly 10-acre property in 2015 for $3.35 million and later rebuilt its Spanish-style home down to the studs, turning the residence into a private retreat in the hills between Malibu and Calabasas. When she listed it in 2021, the home sold within weeks for $6.4 million, above its asking price, according to Observer. Now offered for $7.995 million, the estate is being presented as a secluded Southern California escape, with meadows, mountain views and access to hiking trails. Reports by Realtor.com and Mansion Global detail how a property that began as a renovation project has become a sought-after hacienda-style home. Read on to know more about it here:A quiet ranch above the cityThe Topanga property covers nearly 10 acres, offering a sense of space and privacy that is increasingly rare in the Los Angeles area. The residence itself measures 4,414 square feet and is built in a Spanish hacienda style, with an earthy, relaxed character that complements its hillside surroundings. Approached by a long drive shaded by oak trees, the home sits among lawns, meadows and natural terrain. The setting is a significant part of its appeal. Rather than being surrounded by neighbouring houses, the estate feels tucked into the landscape, with canyon and mountain views and room to explore outdoors, as per reports.The property’s location also offers a balance between seclusion and access. Topanga sits in the mountains between Malibu and the San Fernando Valley, giving residents a more rural atmosphere while remaining within reach of Los Angeles. Its private hiking trails and broad grounds make the estate feel less like a conventional suburban home and more like a personal retreat.A rebuild from the studsZellweger purchased the property in 2015 for $3.35 million. She then undertook an extensive renovation, taking the home down to the studs and rebuilding it, according to the property coverage in Realtor.com and Observer. The phrase suggests a major overhaul rather than a surface-level refresh, with the house reworked to suit its new owner and the lifestyle the land made possible. The finished home includes four bedrooms and five bathrooms. Its interiors mix the rustic warmth associated with Spanish-style architecture with modern comforts and an open layout. A central great room brings together the main living areas, while large windows and doors help connect the interior to the outdoor spaces. The property’s design is oriented around the landscape. Rooms open towards the pool patio, allowing the house to flow naturally into the gardens. The result is a home that feels spacious without losing the intimate character of a hacienda, where shaded outdoor corners and indoor gathering spaces are equally important.Pool, trails and outdoor livingThe reports further suggested that the estate’s outdoor areas are among its defining features. An infinity-edge pool sits beside a patio with an outdoor fireplace, providing a place to unwind while taking in views of the surrounding hills. A pergola and landscaped seating areas add room for dining and entertaining outside. The grounds also include meadows and hiking trails, offering more than a manicured lawn. For a buyer seeking a connection to nature, the land provides space for walks and quiet time without leaving home. The oak-shaded approach and surrounding greenery help reinforce the feeling of a secluded ranch.The primary bedroom opens directly to the pool patio through large sliding glass doors. This indoor-outdoor arrangement is well suited to the Southern California climate, where outdoor living can be part of everyday life for much of the year. The estate’s layout makes the transition between bedroom, patio and landscape feel seamless.A quick sale in 2021After spending about six years at the property, Zellweger listed it for $5.99 million in 2021. The home drew interest quickly and sold for $6.4 million, approximately $400,000 above asking. Observer reported that the sale came roughly a month after the listing, while other coverage said it sold in less than two weeks.The sale price was nearly double what Zellweger had paid in 2015. That difference reflects not only the property’s location and acreage, but also the extensive rebuild she completed during her ownership. The gain does not account for renovation spending, taxes, upkeep or transaction costs, but the fast sale suggested buyers responded to the home’s combination of privacy, design and outdoor amenities.Zellweger sold the ranch in 2021. Four years later, it returned to the market with an asking price of $7.995 million, a notable increase from its previous sale. The listing puts a fresh value on the land and the work carried out on the home, while asking prospective buyers to weigh the appeal of a large, private estate against its premium price.A new chapter for the haciendaThe property’s return to the market comes at a time when buyers may be looking closely at location, privacy and the risks associated with hillside living. Topanga was among the areas threatened by the January 2025 wildfires, and prospective owners of properties in the region may consider factors such as fire preparedness, access and maintenance alongside the home’s design.Still, the ranch offers a distinctive package: nearly 10 acres, a rebuilt hacienda-style residence, a pool and outdoor fireplace, mountain views and private trails. Its appeal rests as much on the surrounding land as on the house itself.For Zellweger, the property was a substantial renovation project and a home she later sold above its asking price. For its next owner, it could become a secluded base in the hills, with room to entertain, walk the trails or simply enjoy the quiet. Listed at $7.995 million, the former ranch is once again looking for someone ready to make the Topanga retreat their own.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: In 1997, Sting bought a 16th-century Tuscan estate as a family retreat; the 865-acre property now produces organic wine, olive oil, honey and fruit
articles.summary: Above the Tuscan town of Figline Valdarno, among the hills of the Chianti Colli Fiorentini, Il Palagio occupies a large stretch of farmland with a history
articles.body: Above the Tuscan town of Figline Valdarno, among the hills of the Chianti Colli Fiorentini, Il Palagio occupies a large stretch of farmland with a history reaching back centuries. The estate became part of Sting and Trudie Styler’s life in 1997, when the couple bought the historic property and began restoring its buildings and agricultural land. What followed was not simply the renovation of a country retreat. The vineyards and olive groves were brought back into use, while new production developed around the estate. Today, Il Palagio operates as a working farm and vineyard, producing wine and olive oil alongside honey, fruit and other crops, while also opening parts of the property to visitors.Il Palagio had centuries of farming history before Sting arrivedIl Palagio was already a substantial agricultural property long before Sting and Styler arrived. Records from the 16th century describe a 350-hectare estate spread across the countryside of the Chianti Colli Fiorentini area. At different points in its history, the land was associated with prominent Italian families and developed the practical features expected of a large rural estate.Agricultural production changed over the centuries. Oil mills, grain stores and wine-making facilities became part of its working life, leaving Il Palagio with a history tied as much to farming as to its architecture. The property that Sting and Styler acquired therefore came with an established agricultural identity, even if much of the work ahead involved restoring it.How Sting and Styler restored Il Palagio as a family retreatSting and Trudie Styler purchased Il Palagio in 1997 and embarked on an extensive restoration of the estate. The work covered the villa as well as the surrounding farm buildings, vineyards and olive groves.For the family, the property became a summer base and a place where they could spend time away from their other homes. Over the years, it was also used for private gatherings, concerts and family occasions. The setting provided a quieter role for a property associated with a globally recognised musician: it became a lived-in country estate rather than simply a historic house.The restoration also had an agricultural side. Rather than separating the residential parts of Il Palagio from the land around them, Sting and Styler developed the estate as a functioning farm.The vineyards begin producing their own wineWine eventually became one of the most visible parts of that agricultural revival. The first vintage of Il Palagio's Sister Moon Toscana IGT was produced in 2007, using grapes grown on the estate itself. The wine marked a point at which the restored property was producing something under its own name rather than simply serving as a private retreat. The estate's output has since extended beyond grapes. Olive oil is produced from its groves, while the farm also produces honey and seasonal fruit including cherries, apricots and peaches.That mix reflects the older character of Il Palagio as a diversified agricultural estate. Its land is not devoted to a single crop, and the farm continues to combine several forms of production.From private retreat to working farmThe transformation has made Il Palagio unusual among celebrity-owned country properties. Its history as a family home remains visible, but the estate also functions as an agricultural operation. The vineyards and olive groves form part of the productive landscape, while other parts of the farm support fruit and honey production. The emphasis on organic farming has also shaped how the estate presents itself today.For Sting and Styler, the property has become closely connected with both their private life and their interest in producing food and wine. The result is an estate where the residential and agricultural sides exist together rather than being treated as separate uses.The estate opens its doorsIl Palagio has gradually become more accessible to visitors. In 2021, a farm shop and pizzeria opened on the estate, giving guests a way to experience its produce without simply visiting as private invitees.The shop offers Il Palagio wines, while the pizzeria adds another food-focused element to the property. Local aperitifs are also used in spritzes served there, bringing some of the surrounding Tuscan food and drink culture into the visitor experience.Then, in 2024, the estate introduced La Taverna dei Lupi, a pop-up street food and music venue in the hills. It opened to the public for the first time that year, with a programme that included performances by both local and international musicians.A family home that still works as a farmIl Palagio has retained its role as a summer home for Sting and Trudie Styler's family, even as more of the estate has been developed for agricultural and visitor use. The villa and its surrounding buildings remain at the centre of the property, with the working landscape extending around them.Its evolution has taken place over decades rather than through a single renovation. The 16th-century estate became a private family base after the 1997 purchase, then developed further as vineyards, olive groves and other forms of production were restored and expanded.The property now combines several identities that have accumulated over its long history: historic Tuscan estate, family home, vineyard, organic farm and visitor destination. Its wine, olive oil, honey and fruit production give the land a working purpose, while the farm shop, pizzeria and seasonal events have created a public-facing side to a place that was once largely private.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida as Category 2 storm, leaves 6 lakh without power
articles.summary: Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday as a Category 2 storm, bringing heavy rain, damaging winds and flooding to parts of the
articles.body: Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday as a Category 2 storm, bringing heavy rain, damaging winds and flooding to parts of the Florida Panhandle and Alabama. More than 664,000 customers in the two states were without power early Saturday as the storm weakened, the Associated Press (AP) reported.The first hurricane of the Atlantic season had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (169 kph) when it struck the Gulf Coast, according to the National Hurricane Center. By early Saturday, Isaias had weakened below hurricane strength as its winds continued to lose intensity.“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, warning that flash flooding would remain a hazard across the region.Flooding, downed trees disrupt communitiesThe storm battered coastal communities known for their white-sand beaches and holiday homes. Roads were flooded in Destin, while police in nearby Pensacola urged residents to stay off the streets because of debris. Images and videos shared online showed fallen trees and power lines, while a video appeared to show a roof being torn off an inn in Pensacola, AP reported.Some counties in Florida's Panhandle temporarily suspended emergency response operations on Friday night because of dangerous conditions.Parts of southern Alabama were also affected, with officials in Mobile reporting fallen trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County in southeastern Alabama were closed because of hazardous conditions.Tim Mowry, a Pensacola resident who rode out the storm at home, said the wind sounded like a train whistle as it blew through a gap in his patio door. He lost power around 4.30 pm but managed to use a generator. Standing water covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were torn down.Despite the damage, Mowry said the storm had been less severe than he had anticipated.“As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate,” he said.He added that his son had tried to drive to his home after losing power but was forced to turn back because fallen trees and power lines blocked the roads.Storm surge and heavy rain pose further risksThe National Hurricane Center warned that storm surges of 3 to 5 feet (0.91 to 1.52 metres) could affect areas stretching from Dauphin Island in Alabama to Florida's Aucilla River.Forecasters also warned of possible tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle and into southern Georgia, as dangerous weather conditions continued to threaten the region.President Donald Trump said the hurricane was “under control” while speaking to reporters at the White House late Friday night after returning from a rally in upstate New York.Isaias was expected to weaken further as it moved inland, although heavy rainfall could continue to cause flooding across parts of the southeastern United States.Authorities urged residents to follow local safety advisories as the storm continued to move through the region.You use AI every day. articles.title: Can police arrest you for protesting? Know your rights and what happens next
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A protest is a constitutionally protected way to express dissent.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A protest is a constitutionally protected way to express dissent. However, the right to assemble peacefully does not mean that demonstrations can take place anywhere or without restrictions. Police and local authorities can regulate gatherings to maintain public order, protect public safety and prevent serious disruption. But they must act within the law, and the mere inconvenience caused by a protest does not automatically justify stopping it or taking participants into custody.So, do you need police permission before holding a protest? Can the police order a peaceful gathering to disperse or detain people who refuse to leave? And what can you do if you believe you have been arrested unlawfully? Here is what the law says about your right to protest and the limits on police powers.Police permission and the right to protest“There is no single, nationwide rule that every protest requires police permission,” said senior advocate Vivek Narayan Sharma. The requirements depend on local laws, the proposed venue and the circumstances. Authorities may require permission or impose conditions relating to the venue, timing, route and size of a gathering.The Constitution protects both freedom of expression and the right to assemble peacefully. Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) guarantee these rights, while Article 19(3) permits reasonable restrictions on public assemblies in the interests of public order and the sovereignty and integrity of India.Sharma said the Supreme Court has recognised the state's responsibility to protect the right to peaceful assembly. As he put it, “the state must actively facilitate peaceful assembly, not merely tolerate it.”In Ramlila Maidan Incident v Union of India, the Supreme Court examined the state's obligations towards a gathering and the limits on police action. The judgment underscores an important distinction: authorities can regulate protests, but they must also respect the constitutional right to hold them.Vishal Gehrana, partner at Karanjawala & Co, said authorities must have a lawful basis for regulating demonstrations.“The authorities may regulate demonstrations to protect public order, public safety, traffic and the rights of others. Such regulation must, however, have a lawful basis and be justified by the circumstances. Preventive powers cannot be used arbitrarily or beyond the purpose for which the law confers them,” he said.When authorities can restrict a demonstrationAuthorities may restrict a protest when there are specific safety concerns, a credible threat to public order or a serious obstruction to essential access. They may also impose restrictions when a valid prohibitory order is in force. However, such measures must be justified by the circumstances, rather than by disagreement with the protesters' views.One provision that authorities can invoke in urgent situations is Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which replaced Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It empowers an Executive Magistrate to issue orders to prevent situations involving danger, obstruction or a disturbance of public tranquillity.Such an order must be in writing and state the material facts justifying it. It ordinarily remains in force for up to two months, although the state government may extend it for a further period of up to six months, subject to the law. An affected person can also apply to have the order withdrawn or modified.Does the existence of such an order automatically make every restriction lawful? No. The reasons for issuing it, its scope and the manner in which it is enforced remain relevant.“An order covering an area or the public generally is not automatically unlawful; its factual basis, scope and operation must be examined,” Gehrana said.In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India, the Supreme Court held that Section 144 orders cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression and that restrictions must be justified, proportionate and open to judicial review.When police can disperse a gathering or take people into custodyPolice can order an assembly to disperse when the legal conditions for doing so are met. Section 148 of the BNSS deals with dispersing unlawful assemblies and certain other gatherings of five or more people that satisfy the statutory conditions concerning public peace.Sharma emphasised that the power to disperse an assembly does not amount to a blanket ban on peaceful protests.“Section 148 BNSS…is a dispersal power, not a blanket prohibition on peaceful protests,” he said.However, ordering a gathering to disperse and arresting its participants are distinct actions. Whether either is lawful depends on the circumstances and the legal grounds invoked. Simply being part of a crowd does not, by itself, establish grounds for arrest.Gehrana said the legality of a mass operation must be assessed individually, rather than on the assumption that the same grounds apply to everyone.“A mass detention is not automatically unlawful merely because several people are taken into custody at the same time. However, the scale of the operation cannot dispense with the requirement for a lawful basis for each person's deprivation of liberty,” he said.Preventive arrest vs preventive detentionPreventive arrest and preventive detention are often used interchangeably, but they refer to different legal powers.Preventive arrest is intended to stop a cognizable offence that police believe is about to be committed. Preventive detention, by contrast, involves detaining a person under a special law, such as the National Security Act, to prevent certain acts considered threatening to public order or national security.Section 170 of the BNSS allows police to arrest a person without a warrant to prevent the commission of a cognizable offence when the statutory conditions are met, including where the offence cannot otherwise be prevented. An arrest under this provision cannot ordinarily be made solely as a precaution: the police must have the required information and grounds for believing that the offence is likely to occur.Custody under Section 170 cannot exceed 24 hours unless further detention is authorised under another legal provision.These powers do not give police unrestricted authority to detain people attending a protest simply because the gathering is inconvenient or may cause disruption. The circumstances and the legal grounds for the action remain decisive.Sharma said preventive powers must be used only for the purposes for which the law grants them. Gehrana similarly stressed that the legality of an arrest depends on the facts, the power invoked and compliance with the applicable safeguards.“The legality of the action depends on the facts, the power invoked and compliance with the applicable safeguards,” Gehrana said.Rights and safeguards after an arrestAn arrest does not strip a person of their basic legal rights. The Constitution and the BNSS provide safeguards that police must follow.An arrested person has the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest and to consult a lawyer of their choice. Article 22(1) of the Constitution protects these rights, while Section 47 of the BNSS requires the arrested person to be informed of the grounds of arrest and, where applicable, their right to bail.Police must also inform a relative, friend or another person nominated by the arrested individual about the arrest and where they are being held. Section 48 of the BNSS sets out this requirement, while Section 53 provides for a medical examination of the arrested person.Another important safeguard is the 24-hour rule. Under Article 22(2) of the Constitution and Section 58 of the BNSS, an arrested person must generally be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the time required for the journey. Further custody requires lawful authorisation.The law also provides specific safeguards for the arrest of women. Under Section 43(5) of the BNSS, a woman should generally not be arrested between sunset and sunrise, except in exceptional circumstances and subject to the prescribed procedure, including prior permission from a magistrate.These protections apply even when police take several people into custody during a protest.“The arrested person must be informed of the relevant rights, and the Magistrate must verify compliance with the applicable requirements,” Gehrana said.Legal remedies if you believe your detention was unlawfulIf you believe you have been unlawfully detained or arrested, you can approach the courts. The appropriate remedy will depend on the circumstances and the legal grounds for your detention.Seek bail or challenge continued custody: Apply to the competent court for bail, where available, or challenge the legal basis for continued detention.File a habeas corpus petition: Approach a high court under Article 226 of the Constitution or, where appropriate, the Supreme Court under Article 32 to challenge unlawful detention.Seek compensation: In appropriate cases, a person whose fundamental rights have been violated may seek compensation. It is not automatic and depends on the facts, evidence and applicable law.The right to protest peacefully is constitutionally protected, but it is subject to lawful and reasonable restrictions. Police can intervene when the law permits them to do so, but they must have valid legal grounds for their actions and comply with the safeguards protecting individual liberty.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2007, Martha Stewart helped launch a New York centre for older adults; a second opened in 2019, bringing more than 20 specialist medical care and wellness services under one roof
articles.summary: Martha Stewart has built a career on recipes, home projects and a business empire. Through all of it, one thing has stayed the same: she cares.
articles.body: Martha Stewart has built a career on recipes, home projects and a business empire. Through all of it, one thing has stayed the same: she cares. She showed it in 2007, when she helped launch the Martha Stewart Center for Living at Mount Sinai Hospital on the Upper East Side. She cared about good food, and she cared about people, especially older people who need the most help. Though her work in New York hospitals gets less attention than her television shows and products, it reaches a group that struggles every day: older adults who manage chronic illnesses, daily tasks and worried families.Martha Stewart Center for LivingIn 2007, she gifted Mount Sinai the Martha Stewart Center for Living. Her inspiration was her mother, Martha Kostyra, who lived an active life until the age of 93. She wanted everyone to enjoy that same sense of well-being as they grew older. The goal was to treat older people as whole individuals, not just as a list of diagnoses.In 2019, a second centre opened downtown at 10 Union Square. Here, patients can see specialists in more than 20 fields, including cardiology, gastroenterology, cancer care, dermatology, orthopaedics and rheumatology. Radiology and physical therapy are also available on site. Think of it as a one-stop shop for wellness as well as treatment.“The idea was simple: give older adults the services and support they need to live with health and dignity,” Nathan Goldstein, MD, professor of geriatrics and palliative medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and chief of geriatrics for Mount Sinai Downtown, said in an earlier release.Care beyond treating illnessesWhat makes the centre unique is its approach to elderly health and care. Instead of just treating illnesses, the centre offers care and wellness programmes. These include tai chi, yoga, music therapy, nutrition planning and fall prevention programmes. The centre also conducts seminars for seniors on various topics, including planning, medication management, depression, long-term care insurance and financial advice.Every new patient receives a full geriatric assessment. Doctors ask about emotional well-being, family support, coping skills and daily functioning, not just medical problems. Each patient is also assigned a social worker. Family members and caregivers can join support groups.“We call it the Center for Living for a reason,” Goldstein said. “We take care of very sick older adults with complicated medical histories, of course, but our goal is ensuring wellness through holistic, interdisciplinary and patient-centred care. And a large part of that is empowering adults aged 65 and older to make their own healthcare decisions and participate directly in their own health maintenance.”Fewer hospital visitsPatients at the Martha Stewart centres have half as many emergency room visits as other older adults, according to Mount Sinai data. Their hospital stays are shorter, and readmissions after a hospital stay are 50 per cent lower. The health system also says the downtown centre recorded nearly 5,000 patient visits in its first year.“We have an incredibly dedicated staff of physicians, nurse practitioners, social workers and others who know our patients beyond their clinical needs. They know the life stories of our patients as well as their families,” Dr Goldstein said.Training the next generationAlong with providing treatment and wellness programmes, the centre also trains doctors. These include medical students, pharmacy residents and postgraduate trainees. articles.title: In 2008, Jamie Oliver launched a programme to teach everyday cooking skills; by March 2024, it had delivered food education to more than 115,000 people in schools and communities across the UK
articles.summary: Learning to cook does not always require expensive ingredients, complicated recipes or professional training.
articles.body: Learning to cook does not always require expensive ingredients, complicated recipes or professional training. Sometimes, knowing how to prepare a simple, balanced meal can make a real difference to everyday life. That was the idea behind Jamie Oliver’s Ministry of Food, a programme launched in 2008 to help people develop practical cooking skills and make healthier food choices. According to the chef’s official website, the first community programme launched in 2008, while the permanent Ministry of Food programme followed in 2009. The initiative grew beyond its original community-based approach, reaching schools and local communities. By March 2024, its food education programmes had reached more than 115,000 people through community and school sites in the UK, Australia and the US, bringing basic cooking knowledge to people who might otherwise have had limited opportunities to learn.How Jamie Oliver’s Ministry of Food beganJamie Oliver, known for his television cooking shows and campaigns around food education, launched the Ministry of Food in Rotherham, England, in 2008. The idea was straightforward: give people the confidence to cook meals from scratch rather than depend heavily on ready-made food and takeaway meals. The programme took inspiration from the British Ministry of Food established during the Second World War, when the government encouraged people to make the most of available ingredients and prepare meals efficiently during food shortages.Oliver adapted that idea for modern life. Instead of focusing on wartime rationing, his initiative aimed to make everyday cooking more accessible and help people understand how food choices could affect their health and wellbeing. The original approach centred on practical demonstrations and hands-on cooking sessions. Participants could learn basic techniques, try recipes and discover that preparing a meal at home did not have to be difficult or time-consuming. The wider goal was to encourage people to pass those skills on to friends and family, allowing cooking knowledge to spread through communities.Teaching skills that people can use at homeThe Ministry of Food focused on practical lessons rather than complicated culinary techniques. Participants were encouraged to learn recipes they could realistically prepare in their own kitchens, using accessible ingredients and straightforward methods. These skills included preparing meals from scratch, handling ingredients, understanding basic cooking techniques and making food choices that supported a balanced diet.For people who rarely cooked, even learning a few reliable recipes could make everyday meal preparation less intimidating. The programme also aimed to show that healthier meals could be prepared without spending excessive amounts of money. The community approach was important because food habits are often shaped by family routines, time constraints, budgets and the knowledge people acquire while growing up. By giving participants the opportunity to cook themselves, the programme sought to build confidence that could continue long after a class ended. The model also encouraged participants to share what they had learnt. Someone who became comfortable preparing a simple meal could introduce the same recipe to a partner, child, friend or neighbour.Taking food education into schools and communitiesOver time, Jamie Oliver’s food education work expanded beyond the original Ministry of Food model. The official website describes community programmes and educational initiatives designed to help more people gain practical food skills. Schools became an important part of that wider effort. Introducing children to food and cooking can help them understand ingredients, develop basic kitchen skills and become more familiar with the meals they eat.Community-based learning offered another route to reach people of different ages and backgrounds. Rather than treating cooking as a specialist skill, the programmes presented it as a useful part of everyday life. The approach also recognised that knowing what constitutes a healthy meal is not always enough. People need the confidence and practical ability to turn that knowledge into food they can prepare at home. By combining food education with hands-on learning, the initiative sought to bridge that gap between understanding healthy eating and putting it into practice.More than 115,000 people reached by 2024According to Jamie Oliver’s foundation’s 2023 Social Impact Report, published in March 2024, its food education programmes had delivered lessons to more than 115,000 people through community centres and schools, with sites in the UK, Australia and the US. The figure reflects the reach of the wider food education work, rather than necessarily representing people taught through the original Ministry of Food programme alone. That distinction matters because Oliver’s food initiatives have developed over the years, with different projects addressing cooking skills, school education and community engagement.The milestone nevertheless illustrates the scale of the effort to make practical food knowledge available to more people. What began with a community-focused programme in 2008 had become part of a broader approach to food education. The number of people reached does not, by itself, establish how many changed their diets or maintained new cooking habits over the long term. However, it shows how the programme’s central idea, teaching people to prepare everyday meals, was carried into a range of educational settings.Why everyday cooking still mattersCooking at home can give people greater control over ingredients, portion sizes and the way meals are prepared. It can also help families make better use of groceries and reduce reliance on prepared food, although the benefits depend on the ingredients, costs and circumstances involved. For children, early exposure to food preparation can help build familiarity with ingredients and encourage participation in family meals. For adults, learning a few dependable recipes can make daily routines easier and give them more options when planning meals on a budget.The Ministry of Food was built around a simple principle: people do not need to become professional chefs to benefit from knowing how to cook. More than a decade after its launch, the programme’s wider legacy lies in its effort to make food education practical, accessible and relevant to everyday life. Its reach by 2024 demonstrates how a community cooking initiative can develop into a broader effort to help people build skills that remain useful well beyond the classroom.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2017, Rihanna's foundation teamed up with a bicycle company to help girls in Malawi get to school; the first bikes arrived as part of a programme pairing transport support with scholarships
articles.summary: For some girls in Malawi, getting to class can mean a long walk each way, adding time and effort to an already demanding school day.
articles.body: For some girls in Malawi, getting to class can mean a long walk each way, adding time and effort to an already demanding school day. In 2017, Rihanna’s Clara Lionel Foundation partnered with bike-sharing company Ofo to address that barrier alongside the cost of education. Their five-year initiative, called 1 KM Action, paired scholarships for girls with bicycles to help them travel to school more safely and quickly. Teen Vogue reported that the first bikes had already arrived in Malawi as the partnership was announced. The idea was simple but practical: a scholarship could help a student afford schooling, while a bicycle could make it easier to get there. Together, the two forms of support aimed to help more girls stay in education. Read more about it here:Tackling two barriers at onceRihanna founded the Clara Lionel Foundation in 2012, naming it after her grandparents. The organisation’s work includes supporting education, health, arts and culture, and emergency response programmes. In 2017, it announced a partnership with Ofo, a Beijing-based bike-sharing company, to support girls pursuing secondary education in Malawi.The collaboration connected two needs that are often treated separately. Scholarships could help students with the costs of continuing their education, while bicycles could ease the challenge of travelling to school. For girls who had to walk long distances, a bike could reduce time on the road and make the daily journey more manageable.The partnership was called 1 KM Action, a name that drew attention to the distance many students travelled. The programme was designed to provide scholarships through the Clara Lionel Foundation’s Global Scholarship Program, while Ofo supplied bicycles for scholarship recipients.In an interview quoted by Teen Vogue, Rihanna said she was pleased that the partnership could help students access quality education and help girls get to school safely, reducing the long walks they might otherwise make alone. The aim was not simply to put bicycles in students’ hands, but to make school attendance more achievable.The first bikes arriveThe first batch of bicycles had arrived in Malawi by the time the partnership was announced. Teen Vogue reported that students and teachers had responded positively to the bikes. Their arrival marked an early step in a collaboration planned to last five years.The bicycles were intended for girls who qualified for scholarships, connecting transport assistance directly to school participation. This made the scheme more targeted than a general bike giveaway. The support was meant to reach students who were continuing their education and facing practical difficulties getting to class.For families, the combined package could address more than one obstacle. Secondary education often involves costs beyond tuition, while the daily commute can require time and energy that might otherwise be spent on study, family responsibilities or rest. A bicycle cannot remove every barrier, but it can change how a student experiences the journey to school.The programme also drew attention to the particular pressures girls can face in accessing education. Long commutes can bring safety concerns and add difficulty to an already demanding routine. By pairing scholarships with bicycles, the initiative acknowledged that school access depends on more than a place in a classroom.Why transport mattersEducation programmes often focus on tuition, supplies or school infrastructure. Yet getting to school is part of the experience too. When a student has to travel a considerable distance each day, the commute can affect attendance, concentration and the time available for other responsibilities.A bicycle offers a relatively direct solution. It can shorten travel time and provide more flexibility than walking, especially where public transport is limited or unreliable. In the context of the 1 KM Action partnership, the bikes were presented as a way to support safer, easier access to school for scholarship recipients.The programme’s design reflected a broader idea: support is most useful when it responds to the daily realities students face. A scholarship may open a door, but practical measures can help students keep walking through it. Combining financial and transport assistance made the initiative more attentive to the full journey from home to classroom.That approach also helped make the partnership visible. The bicycles were a tangible part of the programme, something students could use every day. The scholarship support, meanwhile, addressed the financial side of continuing education, creating a package that connected opportunity with access.A five-year partnershipThe Clara Lionel Foundation and Ofo described 1 KM Action as a five-year partnership. Through the foundation’s Global Scholarship Program, the initiative aimed to help hundreds of girls attend secondary school in Malawi. Ofo’s contribution was to provide bicycles to those receiving scholarships.The arrangement brought together a charitable foundation and a commercial bike-sharing company around a shared goal. The collaboration showed how different kinds of organisations could contribute distinct resources: the foundation focused on educational support, while the company supplied transport.The partnership was part of Rihanna’s wider philanthropic work, but it also responded to a specific local challenge. Rather than treating education as an abstract cause, the initiative linked support to the practical realities of school attendance in Malawi.The first bikes arriving was an important beginning, not evidence that all transportation or education barriers had been resolved. The programme’s long-term value depended on how many students it could support and whether the combined assistance helped them remain in school.A small change with a daily impactA bicycle can seem like a modest intervention compared with the scale of educational inequality. Yet for a student who must travel a long way to class, the difference can be felt every day. Less time walking may mean more time for lessons, homework or rest, while a more manageable journey can ease some of the strain on students and families.The 2017 partnership between Rihanna’s foundation and Ofo was built around that kind of everyday impact. Scholarships addressed the cost of schooling, and bikes helped with the journey. The first batch had already reached Malawi when Teen Vogue reported on the initiative, giving the programme an immediate, practical start.The project offered a reminder that helping students stay in school can involve more than paying fees. It can mean understanding what stands between a young person and the classroom, then finding support that fits the problem. For the girls receiving bicycles and scholarships, 1 KM Action aimed to make the route to education a little shorter, safer and more possible.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘Country governed by Parliament, not streets’: BJP slams oppn, CJP over protests
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday defended the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and accused opposition parties of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday defended the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and accused opposition parties of politicising the exercise following electoral setbacks. Tensions were high in Delhi with seveeral protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Addressing a press conference on Saturday, BJP spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad cited the Supreme Court’s handling of challenges to the SIR process and alleged that the opposition was seeking to build a narrative that India’s democracy was under threat.Prasad said several opposition parties had approached the Supreme Court to challenge the SIR process.“To challenge the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), the Congress, the Trinamool Congress (TMC), and several other parties approached the Supreme Court. Even some of those so-called ‘jhola-chaap’ individuals, also went along,” he said.Referring to the court proceedings, Prasad added, “The Supreme Court heard these petitions repeatedly, and what has it ultimately said? That the SIR process will continue.”He also referred to the deployment of judicial officers to oversee aspects of the electoral process in West Bengal following objections raised by Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee.Prasad alleged that judicial officers faced misconduct during the process, citing an incident involving a woman judicial officer who was reportedly left in tears amid the commotion.“So, the question is: You refuse to accept the authority of the courts, you refuse to trust the votes... you don't trust in democracy, you trust nothing, so what does it mean?” he said.The BJP leader further alleged that the opposition was promoting a narrative about threats to Indian democracy, suggesting that foreign forces were seeking to influence perceptions of the country.“The conclusion being drawn is clear: they only trust in one thing whicch is the influce of foreign forces, they appears to create a narrative that India’s democracy is under threat,” Prasad said.He linked these allegations to India's economic performance under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, pointing to assessments by international financial institutions.“And when does this narrative gain momentum? Often, it is when India is making rapid progress under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Look at the latest assessments from institutions such as the IMF and the World Bank, which have described India as a bright spot in the global economy,” he said.The remarks came amid heightened tensions in the national capital, where around 1,000 protesters had been detained by Saturday while attempting to march towards Jantar Mantar for a Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led demonstration demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Delhi Police sources said told news agency ANI.Referring to the BJP’s electoral victories in Assam, Nandigram and Puducherry, the BJP MP linked the results to the protests that have rocked Delhi and other parts of the country.“Based on the events of today and the preceding three days, two things have become clear. One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by Parliament, not by the streets,” he said.“We are not opposed to protests, but you have weaponised street protests because of your electoral defeats,” Prasad added, targeting opposition parties.Police continued to take demonstrators into preventive custody, informing them that permission had not been granted for the gathering. The latest detentions followed a protest by opposition leaders and MPs of the INDIA bloc on Friday, when they marched from Parliament towards Rashtrapati Bhavan, seeking Kumar’s immediate resignation. A delegation led by Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge also met the President to raise concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition has demanded the suspension and cancellation of the SIR exercise, restoration of millions of names it claims have been deleted from electoral rolls, repeal of legal protections granted to the Chief Election Commissioner, and a return to paper ballots in place of electronic voting machines (EVMs).Security was heightened across parts of central Delhi, with authorities imposing restrictions and detaining several leaders and protesters.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Crompton Greaves Consumer Electricals Ltd. has expanded its kitchen appliances portfolio with the launch of the InstaNourish Pro Multi Purpose Kettle, a compact cooking appliance designed to offer multiple cooking functions including searing, steaming and boiling. The company noted that demand for compact kitchen appliances is increasing as consumers look for convenient ways to prepare home-cooked meals, steam vegetables, boil ingredients, reheat food and make beverages without requiring multiple devices.Designed for versatile cookingAccording to the company, the InstaNourish Pro can be used for preparing a range of foods including rice, steamed vegetables, snacks and reheated meals. The appliance comes with a 600W heating system and a 1.2-litre capacity. Other features include a stainless steel steamer basket, cool-touch body, dry boil protection with automatic shut-off, wide-mouth design for easier cleaning and operation, and an LED indicator to show when the appliance is in use.Crompton said the product is designed to offer greater flexibility to consumers by enabling multiple cooking applications through a single appliance.Anand Kumar N, Business Head, Pumps & Kitchen Appliances at Crompton Greaves Consumer Electricals Ltd., said changing lifestyles and smaller living spaces are influencing how consumers cook at home. "As consumers adapt to changing lifestyles and living spaces, they are looking for greater flexibility in how they prepare meals at home.
